A note before we begin: This week’s newsletter is a special feature from The Ken , based on Episode 2 of Intermission, their deep-dive video podcast on India’s largest companies. This edition looks at Bajaj Finance and how it grew from a small scooter-loan business into one of India’s most important retail-credit giants.
Think back to the last time you bought a smartphone, refrigerator, or TV set. Perhaps you weren’t ready to pay the full ticket price, but you knew instalments were an option. You handed over a modest amount of cash as your first payment, then swiped your EMI Card issued by Bajaj Finance. Minutes later, you were all set. There was no paperwork or waiting days for a credit check. You walked out with your new phone, or your new appliance was ready to be delivered to your home shortly.
This is retail at its most convenient, and there are many mechanisms behind the scenes to keep it that way. It’s the result of one of the most audacious transformations in India’s financial history, beginning with a family feud.
Dynastic split
In 2008, when Rahul Bajaj was the patriarch of the Bajaj Group, the family’s business empire went through a separation. Rahul’s oldest son, Rajiv, got Bajaj Auto, the iconic maker of two-wheelers. His younger son, Sanjiv, was handed Bajaj Auto Finance, a small non-banking lender whose sole purpose was to make it easier for people to buy Bajaj scooters on instalments.
At the time of this split, Bajaj Auto Finance was a footnote to Bajaj Auto, giving out no more than 3,000 loans a day. No one would have said it was an arm of the business with strong prospects for growth, and no one would have bet on it becoming bigger than the company that it was spun out of.
Today, Bajaj Finance gives out 150,000 loans a day. Its market cap of roughly Rs 5.7 lakh crore is more than twice that of Bajaj Auto. It lends for seemingly everything—refrigerators, hair transplants, MRI machines, and business expansion loans. Consider it to be a bank in all but name.
Bajaj Finance’s journey to reach its current state involved counterintuitive thinking, an obsession with data about borrowers, and a retail strategy that reshaped how more than a billion people buy things.
The Citibank accident
Let’s go back to 1986. Scooters were aspirational in India. A Chetak did cost nearly Rs 11,000, equivalent to 31 months of the average Indian’s income. Banks were still largely state-owned and government-directed, so they weren’t interested in financing ordinary people’s purchases of consumer goods. So, if you wanted a scooter, you saved for years until you could pay the full retail price, perhaps with a bit of help from friends and family.
Citibank saw an opportunity. It approached Bajaj to explore co-lending, and executives from both companies wanted to visit any factory to see whether the workers there would be interested in their scooter loans. They chose the Tata Motors factory in Pune and approached Tata’s engineers, who ran the numbers, decided it was too expensive, and passed on the loans.
But then the executives walked into the workers’ canteen to see if they would be interested in their scooter loans, only to find an entirely different reception. Over three days, the executives from Bajaj and Citibank issued loans for 2,000 scooters in that canteen.
The lesson for Bajaj was that people wanted to borrow funds to buy scooters, so they could become lenders for that on their own. In March 1987, Bajaj Auto Finance was formally incorporated as a subsidiary of Bajaj Auto. As The Ken deputy editor Seetharaman G put it in the latest episode of the Intermission podcast, “Unwittingly, Citibank had done a beta test for what became one of India’s most successful lenders.”
Zero per cent, zero competition
The 1990s brought liberalisation, and a wave of foreign financial companies entered India, all clawing their way into the consumer-durables market. Citibank, GE Money (then called Countrywide), Kotak, and ICICI were all in the business of financing TVs and fridges. Kotak pioneered the first “0% EMI” plan, which charged a 2% processing fee but was promoted as interest-free.
For Indians who wanted to spend their hard-earned money on new products, the cost of credit fell dramatically, from 24% interest charged by informal shopkeepers in the 1980s to Countrywide’s 16%, then to effectively 0% by the late 1990s. After that, the major players left this space. The loans were simply too small and too complex to administer, so they weren’t worth the effort for companies such as Citibank or GE Money, which had their eyes trained on loans with much higher denominations.
By the mid-2020s, Bajaj Finance had the consumer-durables financing market almost entirely to itself.
The store is the branch
Bajaj Finance then did something that no bank had made the effort to do. It went where the customers were.
Croma, the retail chain with stores around India, opened its first locations in 2006. Bajaj Finance made itself indispensable from the get-go, ensuring that wherever a customer needed credit, it was also there to make the offer.
Meanwhile, Nilesh Gupta, the managing director of Vijay Sales, said Bajaj’s Finance share of financing at his stores has never dropped below 50%, even when there were four or five competing lenders. And Bajaj Finance has never demanded exclusivity, because it knows it doesn’t have to.
Its major advantage is data. Bajaj Finance tracks when customers last bought a refrigerator or washing machine. When the appliance is seven or eight years old, Bajaj Finance goes to Croma or Vijay Sales and tells them: Here are 50,000 customers who are likely thinking about replacing a big-ticket appliance soon. If the stores.
There’s also a major distinction in the way engagement with customers played out. A former Croma executive told Seetharaman G that his company’s relationship with a customer ends with the sale; any message that Croma sends the customer after that moment is treated as spam. A payment acknowledgement sent by Bajaj Finance, on the other hand, is opened and read, because it’s about the customer’s money. Offers for the next product can be placed in that message, and there’s a good chance they’ll be read.
The EMI card
By the mid-2020s, Bajaj Finance wanted to make it even easier for customers to borrow. The lender had already serviced borrowers around India, and those who came for a second, third, or fourth loan were being put through the same process as a new applicant. Even a wait of three hours, a significant improvement from processing that took up to five days, was too much for some customers and led to complaints. After all, if Bajaj Finance had all their personal details, why was there still a holdup?
A credit card could solve that problem, but Bajaj Finance couldn’t issue them. Only banks could do that. So, the company itself invented the next best thing: the EMI Card, or the Existing Member Identification Card. Its forced acronym led most customers to associate the card with equated monthly instalments, which suited Bajaj Finance just fine.
Cardholders were pre-approved for loans on 20–40 product categories. That meant they could walk into a store, tap the card, and get a loan decision in minutes. Bajaj Finance also went to point-of-sale terminal operators such as Pine Labs and Atos, and asked them to calibrate their machines to accept the EMI Card alongside major credit cards.
Consider what this meant. Bajaj Finance’s product started out as a scooter loan, but then became the lending infrastructure underneath India’s consumer economy. Its data flywheel was composed of a customer buying, repaying, and then buying again, with the company learning more about them at every turn.
Continued growth, continued evolution
It should come as no surprise that some categories of lending got bigger, and bigger, and bigger. Bajaj Finance spun out mobile phones, furniture, fitness equipment, luxury watches, and groceries as its own verticals. Each new vertical was handled by its own team, which formed its own partnerships and had its own growth targets. Once, Big Bazaar ran an EMI programme with Bajaj Finance, with the acronym referring to both the card offered by Bajaj Finance and equated monthly instalments. Within months, 200,000–250,000 people signed up.
Bajaj Finance also became obsessive about costs. Its CEO, Rajeev Jain, who joined up after a decade at GE Money and other foreign lenders, was known to spend weekends reviewing the underwriting cost of loans against property, taking it from Rs 45,000 per loan down to Rs 8,000. The consumer-durables arm saw this and trimmed its own processing costs from Rs 1,200 to Rs 800 per loan. Since Bajaj Finance was issuing 200,000 consumer-durables loans per month, that translated to Rs 8 crore of savings every 30 days.
All of this is impressive. Bajaj Finance was able to grow at blistering speed and constantly enter new categories, all while taking costs down in processes that were key to its business. This is a feat that few companies can accomplish.
The full story
Bajaj Finance went from being a footnote in Bajaj Auto’s annual report to a company worth twice as much as the parent it was spun out of. It became a crucial part of lending for Indians at every stage of their adult lives.
But it’s so much more. A rough inheritance fight nearly broke the Bajaj business dynasty. Rajeev Jain’s leadership style as CEO changed the company's culture. And if you look closely enough, Bajaj Finance is far more than meets the eye.

A chart showing the rupee’s fall against the dollar over the last 15 years is making the rounds on Twitter this week. The caption said the rupee has lost 50% of its value and that “for the middle class, that is like losing half your retirement, half your savings, and half your purchasing power.”
Source: Twitter
The chart is accurate. In 2011, a dollar cost about ₹45. Today, it costs roughly ₹96. The rupee lost more than half of its value in 15 years. But the recent pace has been sharper than usual.
If you look, over the past two decades, the rupee has depreciated by roughly 3.5-4% per year against the dollar. But in just the last year, it has gone from the mid-80s to the mid-90s. That is about 12% in one year, well above the long-term average, which explains why sentiment is negative.
The more important question that I want to discuss in this Second Order edition is: has your money really lost half its value as the post suggests?
It depends on what you are spending it on.
When your money value comes down
If you are saving in rupees and spending in dollars, yes. Without a doubt.
Say, a New York trip in 2011 cost $2,000, which was equivalent to ₹90,000 back then. The same trip today would be double just because of the weaker rupee, even without considering any inflation.
What if you held that initial ₹90,000 in cash from 2011? At today's exchange rates, it is worth only about $940. It has quite literally halved in dollar terms.
So, yeah, if you have a child who plans to study abroad, or a medical procedure planned overseas, the rupee’s fall has made those goals more expensive in rupee terms. For any financial goal in a foreign currency, the depreciation is a direct hit.
When the rupee depreciation does not impact
Now flip it. What if your spending is entirely within India?
You earn in rupees, buy groceries in rupees, and pay rent in rupees. Would the rupee’s fall against the dollar halve your savings?
No. If a kilo of premium basmati rice costs ₹60 in 2011 and costs ₹140 today, that is domestic inflation at work.
So, in this case, to say that your money in India lost value because of the rupee depreciation is not entirely true.
Your purchasing power declined over 15 years, but not because of the exchange rate; rather, due to domestic inflation (averaging 5 to 6% per year).
That said, the exchange rate plays a role in domestic inflation.
Imported inflation
See, India is not a closed economy. We import a lot of what we consume. When the rupee weakens, importers pay more rupees for the same dollar-priced commodity. Some of that cost reaches you.
This happens in two ways.
The first is direct. Say, you imported whey protein, the olive oil from Spain, and the phone whose chips were made abroad. These were priced in foreign currency at some point. When the rupee weakens, the importer’s costs rise. Your retail price follows.
The second is indirect. India imports about 85% of its crude oil. A weaker rupee makes that oil costlier in rupee terms. Higher oil prices feed into diesel. Diesel feeds into transportation. Transportation feeds into the price of everything that moves by truck, which is essentially everything. Your tomatoes are not imported. But the diesel that brought them to your city is linked to imported crude. Your dal is Indian. But the fertiliser in the soil had imported raw materials.
How much actually passes through?
Less than what most people imagine.
When I asked my roommate (with no finance background) what image came to mind when she repeatedly heard “rupee depreciation,” she imagined people standing in long queues outside petrol pumps, holding bundles of cash, struggling to buy basic things.
That is the extreme image. Currency depreciation alone does not create that kind of crisis. That happens when a falling currency combines with deeper problems: a shortage of dollars, already high inflation, heavy external borrowings, weak political stability, or panic.
India’s situation is different. The rupee’s fall does push up prices, but not rupee-for-rupee.
Economists have a term for this: exchange rate pass-through. It is simply asking, if the rupee falls 10%, how much of that 10% actually shows up in what you pay at the store?
An article on the RBI website talks about this scenario in India. A rule of thumb it highlights is that if the rupee falls by 10%, prices will rise by about 0.7 percentage points.
So yes, rupee depreciation can pass through into inflation. But in normal conditions, it usually does not pass through as dramatically as people fear.
So where does this leave you?
If your future expenses are denominated in a foreign currency, depreciation directly reduces the value of your savings. You simply need more rupees to buy the same dollars or euros.
If your spending is mostly in India, the impact is smaller, but it still exists through imported inflation. How much you feel it depends on what you consume.
1. Match the currency of your investments with the currency of your goals
If you have goals tied to foreign currency, such as:
Child’s education abroad
International travel
Overseas medical expenses
Invest in international assets to match those goals. When the rupee weakens, your dollar investments rise in rupee terms. Once the investment currency and goal currency match, the exchange rate impact no longer matters. You have naturally hedged the goal.
2. Even if all your goals are in India, consider international exposure
When we talk about international investing, most people think it is about getting access to companies and sectors we do not have in India and being part of their growth: AI, semiconductor manufacturers, big tech platforms, and global luxury brands.
But it is also currency diversification and geopolitical diversification. A part of your portfolio in foreign assets protects you from some of the future rupee depreciation.
If you cannot invest internationally right now for whatever reason, at the very least, factor in depreciation in your financial planning.
For example, say your child’s university in the US costs $50,000 a year today, which is equivalent to Rs 48 lakh. The tuition itself might increase by 3 to 4% each year. But on top of that, the rupee could weaken another 4% annually. In total, you have to provision for 8% hike every year, at the least.
For domestic goals like retirement, if you are worried that the future is going to be worse, increase your inflation assumption by about one percentage point. Instead of 6%, plan for 6.5%-7%. That gives you a buffer against imported inflation over the long term.
3. Does gold help when the rupee falls?
Gold is widely known as an excellent currency hedge.
Gold is globally priced in US Dollars ($ per ounce). Because of this, it has an inverse relationship with the rupee. When you buy gold in India, you are indirectly buying a dollar-denominated asset.
If the global price of gold remains unchanged but the rupee weakens against the dollar, the price of gold in India will still rise.
This is why gold can help when the rupee falls.
But there is one thing to remember.
If global gold prices fall sharply, the benefit from rupee depreciation may not be enough.
Say the rupee weakens by around 10%, but global gold prices also fall by around 10%. In that case, you may not really gain much in rupee terms because one cancels out the other.
The same applies to international stocks.
When the rupee falls, your foreign investments look better in rupee terms. But if you bought those investments at very high prices, and the underlying stocks fall sharply, the currency benefit may not save you.
Needless to say, rupee appreciation can have the opposite effect on the value of your investments.
One last thing..
A falling rupee is not always bad.
Importers may struggle. Exporters may gain. People with foreign goals may need to save more. People who already own foreign assets may see some benefit.
So within the economy, a falling rupee creates both winners and losers.
What matters to you as an individual comes down to three things. Do you earn in rupees or dollars? Do you spend in India or abroad? And do your investments have any foreign exposure?

In a perfect world, a central banker wants three things:
Independent monetary policy.
This is the ability to set interest rates to manage domestic inflation and growth. If it sees the domestic economy slowing down, it should be able to cut interest rates to spur activity and not worry about what the US Fed (their central bank) is doing.
Stable exchange rate
This gives confidence to businesses to trade across borders without worrying that the currency will swing 10% overnight. For instance, if you’re an Indian company importing machinery from Germany, and the rupee swings 10% in a month, your cost projections go out the window. So stability matters for trade confidence.
Free Capital Flow
Allowing money to move in and out of the country without friction to attract foreign investment. Or put another way, this allows a country to fund infrastructure using global savings. And when foreign investors can move money freely and quickly, it makes the country an attractive destination.
But in the real world, the Mundell-Fleming Trilemma kicks in.
And I’ll explain what that is.
So in the early 1960s, economists Robert Mundell and Marcus Fleming, both independently, had a similar thought — they wanted to figure out how these three aspects of economic policy could work together if at all. Remember, this was a time when most currencies were pegged to the US dollar (because of the Bretton Woods system but I won’t dive into that now), so it was quite crucial to understand how everything was linked.
And they came to the realisation that central bankers can’t have their cake and eat it too. There was a trade-off involved and in reality they could only pick two. If you try to grab the third, the other two will eventually break.
Sidebar: Mundell won the Nobel Prize in Economics in 1999 for his work on this trilemma. If you ask why Fleming was not included in this award, I’m not entirely sure other than to assume that it’s only because the Prize isn’t awarded posthumously.
Sketched out, it looked like this. Although in those days, the focus was on a “Fixed” Exchange Rate, I’ve replaced it with “Stable Exchange” rate here for all intents and purposes.
But let’s try and understand this better with India as an example. And this is a very crude and simplistic explanation.
Say the Indian economy is facing an economic slowdown. But inflation is stable and prices are controlled. So the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) decides to cut interest rates to boost growth.
Low interest rates will hopefully nudge everyone to borrow and spend money. Also, the RBI might choose to increase the supply of money in the economy — one way to do it is by telling banks to maintain lower levels of reserves and lend out the excess money. So now we have a situation of lower interest rates and a higher money supply.
Meanwhile, let’s assume that across the seas, the US Fed is facing inflation so it has kept its interest rates higher.
Now, if capital can flow freely — which it can for the most part in India —, what do foreign investors do?
They’ll easily start withdrawing their money out of India, where returns are lower, and park it in the US, where returns are higher.
It’s just rational.
But as they pull out, they don’t want rupees anymore. They want dollars. Which means they’re selling rupees and converting it into dollars. There’s a supply of rupees and demand for dollars. And the classic demand-supply equation says that when supply > demand, the price falls. In this case, the rupee weakens against the dollar.
So it falls from ₹80/$ to ₹95/$.
Sure, there’s a positive spin to a weaker rupee which I’ve written about earlier , but it doesn’t help importers in India. They have to shell out more rupees to get things into the country. And since India is an import-dependent nation, our bills add up quickly.
So if the RBI wants to keep the exchange rate stable in this scenario, it has two options.
It can either use its dollar reserves to buy rupees and prop the currency up — which it does constantly. But when the RBI takes rupees out of the system in exchange for those dollars, it reduces the amount of cash circulating in the Indian banking system. That hurts the economy’s growth push.
Or the RBI can raise interest rates back up to attract foreign investors and pump up the demand for rupees that way, but then it has lost its monetary policy independence. It’s no longer setting rates for India’s needs. It’s setting them to keep pace with the US.
See the problem?
Each side of the triangle is pulling against the other two. You can fix any two sides, but the third side will buckle under the pressure.
For instance, if we want a stable exchange rate and autonomy with interest rate decisions, then we need to compromise on free capital flows. Like China. The country keeps a tight leash on the yuan’s exchange rate, and it runs its own monetary policy. But to do both, it has to restrict capital flows. It controls how money moves in and out of the country. This works, but it also means the yuan isn’t freely convertible, and that’s precisely why China has struggled to position it as a global reserve currency. You can’t be the world’s money if the world can’t freely use your money.
Source: Bloomberg
On the other hand, if we want free capital flows and a stable exchange rate, then we need to follow the Hong Kong model. It pegs the Hong Kong dollar tightly to the US dollar — it has stayed between 7.75 and 7.85 HKD per USD since 2005.
Capital flows freely in and out of the financial hub. But to maintain that peg, Hong Kong has essentially given up its monetary policy. Its central bank is forced to mirror whatever the US Fed does, even when that might not be what Hong Kong’s own economy needs.
This is in fact what the Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA) said just last week:
The future trend of US interest rates is quite uncertain, which may influence the interest rate environment in Hong Kong. The public should carefully manage interest rate risks when making decisions about property purchase, investment or borrowing.
You have to give up something for the other two.
Of course India tries its best to deftly navigate all three corners. But it’s constantly making choices.
When the RBI lets the rupee fall, it’s effectively saying we care more about domestic growth and interest rate control right now than about the exchange rate. That helps borrowers and businesses that rely on cheap credit. But it hurts importers, raises the price of oil (which India largely imports), and chips away at the purchasing power of ordinary people. When the RBI defends the rupee by burning through reserves, it’s saying the opposite that stability matters more right now, even if it costs us.
It all depends on what moment we’re in, what the economy needs, and what pressures are building up.
That’s the trade off.

For most middle-class Indians, what we do for a living is not just about a source of income. It is, in many ways, how we define ourselves. At family gatherings, at weddings, in casual introductions, the question that follows your name is almost always about your job. Your profession is your identity, your social standing, your proof that the years of education paid off (whether we like it or not).
And for a long time, the journey to get there has followed a familiar script. Get educated. Find a stable job. Hold on to it. Build a life around that stability.
Even today, that instinct has not gone away. Every now and then, we see news covering how a large number of applicants are chasing a limited number of jobs. For many families, just getting a job, any job with a predictable salary, is still the milestone.
At the same time, there is also a visible shift. Being loyal to one company for decades also seems outdated now. More people are experimenting, switching careers, and freelancing.
So both realities exist together. The old script and the new one are running in parallel. And we cannot say which force is bigger.
A recent book by Saurabh Mukherjea* (Chief Investment Officer of Marcellus Investment Managers), Breakpoint, explores the former. The book’s larger argument is about consumption, which, in simple terms, is the spending that people do in an economy.
When you buy groceries, pay school fees, eat out, take a holiday, buy a phone, all of that adds up to what economists call private consumption. It accounts for roughly 60% of India’s GDP, making it the single biggest engine of the economy. And the middle class, the group earning between ₹5 lakh and ₹1 crore a year (as per Mukherjea’s definition), has historically been the group doing most of that spending.
Apparently, the salaried, tax-paying middle class does not just consume; it also employs and provides livelihoods to a far larger population below it. So when this formally employed group comes under pressure, the ripple effects are far bigger.
Mukherjea’s thesis is that there have been structural changes in the financial lives of this group over the past several years. And when they are under pressure, consumption slows. If consumption slows, growth slows. And that is when policy intervention becomes necessary. That is the arc of the book.
As a personal finance writer, what stood out to me were the trends in middle-class income and rising borrowing, which are essentially just two chapters of the book.
Just a note: this is not a substitute for reading the book. A lot of nuance can be missed when one person picks up a few threads from a 200-page argument. Nor am I suggesting that everything in here is gospel. These are the author’s arguments, supported by the data he has chosen to highlight.
With that, let us get into the first idea: how our income growth has not kept pace with inflation. Or to put it simply, the plate of responsibilities, your expenses, your commitments, remains the same or is only getting bigger. But the roti on that plate, your income, is shrinking.
Real wages and the cost of being middle class
In the last few years, it’s common to see students getting placement offers during campus recruitment but never receiving a joining date. For a variety of reasons, landing a job after education has become tougher.
There is also a counterintuitive pattern here. Our friends at The Daily Brief recently did an episode on how unemployment in India is actually higher among the educated than among the less educated. That is a strange sentence to read, but the data supports it.
So that is the setting. Jobs are hard to come by, and the ones we have are harder to keep because of newer technologies and global uncertainties.
But what about the people who sustain this? Are their salaries at least keeping up? Here’s what the book says.
Between FY2016 and FY2025, the average salary cost per employee at the Nifty 50 companies, India’s fifty largest listed firms, went from roughly ₹10.07 lakh to ₹10.95 lakh. That is a CAGR of just about 1%. Over the same period, the government-reported inflation rate ran at about a 5% CAGR. Which means, in real terms (that is, income adjusted for inflation), employees at India’s biggest companies saw their purchasing power fall by roughly 4% every year for eight years.
See, the average could also be pulled down if companies hired more people at junior levels or lower-wage roles. But the book assumes the increments have been lower, which is also a possibility.
Anyway, this is about the Nifty 50 companies. The best of the best. The broader picture is even more sobering. Analysis of Income Tax Department data cited in the book shows that the tax-paying cohort earning between ₹5 lakh and ₹1 crore saw its average income rise from ₹10.23 lakh to ₹10.69 lakh over 11 years. A CAGR of 0.4%. Not four per cent. Zero point four.
The book also quotes Deloitte India, pointing out that India ranks among the bottom 25% of 130 countries in real wage growth.
Now, on the other side of the equation is the cost of living.
The inflation the government reported (CPI numbers in the past) assumes about 50% of our spending goes towards food. But that is not the case for most of us. We spend on education, hospitals, restaurants, clothes, vacations, vehicles, and a lot more.
As per Mukherjea’s calculation, when you account for all of this, the effective inflation for a middle-class household comes closer to 9%. Going by that, the growth in incomes, after adjusting for inflation, is even worse than the above numbers suggest.
To rub salt into the wound, the income tax burden on the middle class also went up. By FY2024-25, according to the book, corporate tax collected by the government had come down to 3.0% of GDP while individual income tax had risen to 3.6%. The underlying assumption in the book was that the individual taxpayers had to fill in the gap created by the loss in revenue from corporates.
So the picture that emerges is this: your salary is barely keeping up, the cost of everything from school fees to hospital bills is climbing faster than your paycheck, and on top of that, the taxes.
Debt: the coping mechanism
The book poses a simple question at this point. If middle-class India is operating in a punishing job market where jobs are hard to come by, and wage growth is elusive, while the cost of living doubles every eight years or so, what is the most likely coping mechanism?
The answer, in one word, is debt.
And going by the data in the book, the Indian middle class has become one of the most indebted groups of people in the world .
And what’s more concerning is that the rise in debt in India has largely been in ‘unproductive’ borrowing. Let me explain.
When someone takes a home loan, they are borrowing to buy an asset that (usually) appreciates over time. That is productive debt. But non-housing debt, personal loans, credit card debt, and consumer EMIs are mostly unproductive. It does not build an asset. You borrow to buy something that loses value the moment you swipe or tap. And it is this category of debt that has gone up.
More and more people have been taking loans to go on a vacation, to buy a phone, or to improve their lifestyle or for genuine necessities.
The book estimates that, for many households, 40% of annual income now goes to repaying the existing debt. And roughly 5 to 10% of India’s retail borrowers, by the book, are in what can only be called a classic debt trap: using multiple loans to finance day-to-day living.
So, the book points out that there is a general acceptance of debt and an extensive use of it in society than before.
Stepping back
Now, I want to make a big note here.
Any narrative built on data can lean in one direction. How the data is interpreted shapes the story. It all depends on the assumptions you make when analysing the data.
Also, the arguments in the book are based on aggregate numbers. The Indian economy is not a single story. It has never been. Some sectors are struggling while others are booming. Some cities are stagnating while others are growing. Your individual reality may look nothing like the averages presented in this book.
I discuss these ideas from the book, not to alarm, but to nudge ourselves to ask some important questions.
How much has our income grown in the last five to ten years? And how much has our lifestyle grown in the same period? Is debt quietly creeping into spaces where it did not exist before, a phone here, a vacation there, an EMI you took because the monthly number looked small? Are we, without quite realising it, part of the broader structural shift that this book describes?
Whatever the past has been, the reality before us feels uncertain in ways it has not been before.
The best advice we keep hearing is to stay curious and to keep upgrading ourselves with new skills. That may be the most reliable way to keep our earning power relevant.
And when it comes to money, I guess all those old sayings become even more important now, like saving for a rainy day, and living within our means, essentially to cut our coat according to our cloth.

A few weeks ago, the ₹40 crore retirement number was doing the rounds on social media. Some people thought it was reasonable. Others thought it was outrageous. Both sides had a point. Whether ₹40 crore is too much, too little has no universal answer.
It depends entirely on the life you are living and the life you want to keep living once the salary stops. It’s individual-specific, which is probably why it makes for such a good debate.
But the episode got me thinking about something else. These retirement numbers — ₹2 crore, ₹5 crore, ₹40 crore — they feel overwhelming. The thought of saving in crores can actually scare us into not starting at all. In fact, a study shows that when a goal feels too large for our brains to process, we tend to freeze rather than act.
So, instead of chasing a precise target number, what if someone just saved a fixed percentage of their income towards retirement every month?
Let’s start with 10%. Would that be enough?
What is “enough”?
Before we test the 10% rule, we need a yardstick.
Based on research on Indian market returns and inflation patterns , a useful rule of thumb is: your retirement corpus should be roughly 33 times your expected annual expenses at retirement.
For example, if your annual expenses at retirement are ₹12 lakh (₹1 lakh a month), you need a corpus of about ₹4 crore. If your expenses are ₹24 lakh a year (₹2 lakh a month), you need about ₹8 crore. Just multiply by 33.
At that size, you can start withdrawing about 3% in the first year of retirement. And in the consequent years, you can increase your withdrawals by whatever the inflation is in the country. By doing so, you can maintain the lifestyle you had at the time of retirement, and the money lasts about 30 years.
This is the 33x rule.
By the way, as per research, this number is conservative enough to survive most, if not all, economic scenarios such as market downturns, inflation spikes, and prolonged low-return phases.
With that, let’s dive in.
The contributions
I wanted to keep this close to reality, so I am focusing on the career growth of a typical Indian urban employee.
A person starts working at 25 with a salary of ₹5 lakh per year.
From 25 to 30, there is no retirement investing. These are the years of finding your feet: clearing education loans, supporting family, setting up a household, or simply living the life you could not afford as a student. During these five years, the salary could roughly double from ₹5 lakh to ₹10 lakh, growing at about 14-15% annually. The steep climb of an early career.
From 30 to 45, these are the years when our earnings peak. Salary grows at about 9-10% annually. This increment number is based on the industry averages that we have seen in the last few years.
From 45 to 50, say, growth slows to about 6%. By 50, salary is about ₹56 lakh.
From 50 to 60, I assumed just 2% annual growth. In a world of AI, assuming generous salary growth all the way to 60 may not be prudent. By 60, salary reaches about ₹68 lakh.
Let’s say retirement expenses are at 50% of that final salary, it works out to about ₹34 lakh per year. The 33x target corpus, then, is roughly ₹11.2 crore. That is the number we are trying to hit.
Is 10% savings enough?
Retirement investing starts at 30 and runs until 60. Every year, 10% of salary is invested in a portfolio that earns 12% returns.
The result is that you would have a corpus of about ₹6.25 crore at age 60. This is against the required ₹11.2 crore, which is a shortfall of nearly ₹5 crore. It’s nowhere near the required 33 times.
*calculation assumes investments are made once a year at year-end, for simplicity purposes.
So what about saving 15%? At 15%, the corpus grows to about ₹9.4 crore. Better, but still about ₹1.9 crore short.
To actually hit 33 times with a fixed savings rate, you would need to save about 18% of income consistently from age 30 to 60.
This is, of course, assuming that all goes as planned.
But what if you step it up?
Now, telling someone to put away 18% of their income for retirement right when they are starting out is a tough ask.
In our example, someone earning ₹10 lakh a year takes home about ₹83,000 a month. Asking them to set aside ₹15,000 of that just for retirement is easier said than done.
The thirties are when most of life happens. Marriage, kids, a home loan, maybe a car, parents who need help, and the vacation to stay sane. Money comes in, money goes out. There is not a lot of room left for retirement while saving for other financial goals.
And you know what, there is actually research that highlights this. It is called “The Life-Cycle Model Implies That Most Young People Should Not Save for Retirement.”
The title sounds extreme, but the idea is that a rupee you save at 30, when you are earning ₹10 lakh, pinches a lot more than the same rupee saved at 45, when you are pulling in ₹42 lakh.
So the paper says, maybe it is okay to save less when you are young and make up for it later when your income can handle it.
Now, let us not get too carried away with that. Saving and investing are still important. The paper assumes people will actually ramp up their savings later.
On those lines, one of the best ways to actually make this work, we think, is the step-up approach. Simply put: increase your savings rate as your income grows.
So we tested it. Start with just 5% at age 30. Increase it by 10% every year until 50. Then freeze it there and continue till 60.
Starting at 5% is manageable. And by the time the rate has climbed to 34%, your income has grown enough that it no longer hurts as much.
With this approach, the corpus at 60 comes to about ₹10.9 crore — roughly 32 times your annual expenses. It doesn’t hit our target of 33x. But it gets much, much closer than 10% or 15% ever did.
If you increase the saving rate well beyond the age of 50, reaching the target would be much easier.
Of course, there are risks with this approach, too. The big one is that this only works if your income keeps going up. If your career hits a wall at 45, or something unexpected happens in your fifties, the plan won’t hold up the same way.
And it works the other way too. If you get a big jump in salary late in your career, you will get used to that lifestyle. But your corpus was built when you were earning much less. It has not caught up with your new life.
Conclusion
Look, all of this depends on what assumptions you take. How fast your career grows, what returns you get, and what life decides to throw at you. And I totally agree that this analysis here is a super simplified version without considering taxes and that our life doesn’t feel the same as in an Excel sheet.
But the point I want to make is that if someone tells you “just save 10% for retirement and you will be fine”, now you know that is not really how it works. The situation worsens if you rely entirely on non-equity assets like a provident fund. It protects your principal, but may require a much higher savings rate, because lower-return assets reduce the compounding available over long periods.
And if saving a big chunk feels impossible right now, take the ‘step-up’ idea seriously. Start with whatever you can. Even 5%. Just commit to nudging it up every year. It is doable, realistic, and gets you a lot closer than staying at a flat number forever.
With a fixed percentage, the absolute amount you save grows automatically as your salary increases (e.g., 10% of ₹50,000 is ₹5,000, but 10% of ₹2,00,000 is ₹20,000).
What a fixed percentage doesn’t change is your savings rate (intensity). As people advance in their careers, their disposable income usually grows much faster than their basic living expenses. A step-up strategy takes advantage of this by increasing the percentage itself (e.g., moving from saving 10% to 15% to 20%).
But that means you have to actually ramp up in the later years without letting lifestyle expenses eat into the surplus.
One more thing I keep coming back to. The step-up changes how you look at your own career.
I think most of us, at some point, have checked what hike or increment our peers got and compared it with what we got. Not saying that is blasphemy. It is only natural.
But when we look at it through the lens of your financial goals, the step-up approach to investing raises a different question. It shifts from “am I earning enough compared to others?” to “is my income growing enough for what I need down the line?”
That is a very different feeling. And weirdly, a much better motivator to think about your own career path and keep it on track.

In the 1980s, China’s per capita income was roughly the same as India’s. The country had faced decades of political chaos — farmer strife, violence under the leader Mao Zedong, and poverty. ~ 90% of the country lived in extreme poverty.
It was, by almost any metric, starting from the same place we were. Or worse.
Cut to today, and China’s per capita income is 5 times that of India’s. It manufactures everything — from the phone in your pocket to the solar panel on your roof to the active ingredients in your paracetamol tablet. It is the second largest economy in the world and it has moved beyond cheap goods to making EVs, semiconductors.
And India?
We’re still debating whether we can get manufacturing’s share of GDP past 15%.
So, on Saturday (the 16th of May) we sat down with Manoj Kewalramani, Chairperson at The Takshashila Institution, and an expert on all things China to understand the country’s rise and rise and rise.
This was part of Zerodha’s offline learning series, Bootcamp. You can keep a track of all our events here .
Kashish Kapoor (left) and Nithin Sasikumar (centre) from Zerodha moderating the session with Manoj Kewalramani (right) of the Takshashila Institution
And I thought I’d use what we learnt from Manoj and weave in bits and pieces that I discovered when I went down rabbit holes subsequently — such as Singapore’s and Japan’s influence on China.
To be honest though, this is more of a Tell Me How than a Tell Me Why ; a how did China become the factory of the world narrative, but, you could also reframe it in your head as a why India lost out on manufacturing story when viewed through the lens of what China did that we didn’t.
Although, do keep in mind that tracing China’s manufacturing story in roughly 4,000 words (yes, I know it’s long; really long) is a tall order. It’s not a comprehensive history but simply a starting point that should hopefully intrigue you into diving further into this topic on your own.
With that preamble out of the way, let’s begin.
The Mao era
A brief history you need to know about China is that for over 2,000 years, the country has been under imperial rule. Various dynasties ran the show. But in 1911, the then ruling Qing dynasty was finally overthrown.
However, it didn’t result in the communists coming to power immediately. At first, the country fragmented as multiple factions took over. And then, in the 1920s, a civil war broke out between the Nationalists (Kuomintang/KMT) and the Communists (CCP).
It took a world war, a Japanese invasion, and two decades for the CCP to actually gain power. Mao Zedong and the CCP officially took over in October of 1949.
And that set in motion a series of changes that would serve as a catalyst in the late 70s.
See, Mao wanted China to become a massive steel producer. So he doubled down on building steel capacity. All state-owned of course. There was no private business at all. Everything was eliminated.
And these functioned in such a manner that families lived inside factory compounds. Your child went to school there. You got married there. Your entire life revolved around the state factory you were assigned to.
But Mao had lofty goals for steel production. And when the factories were deemed not to be enough, he ordered the infamous “backyard steel furnaces. This meant that every village was given a production quota — and villagers melted their tools and utensils just to keep things going.
But backyard smelting didn’t yield steel that could be used for massive infrastructure and most of this went to waste.
Meanwhile, resources that could’ve gone into farming also went into steelmaking. And agriculture began to take a back seat.
But Mao’s government set quotas for procuring grains too.
And that became a problem. Remember, there was no private ownership of lands either. It was collective farming. But collectivism didn’t result in higher yields either. And on top of that, local CCP officials didn’t want to be seen as a failure so they lied to the top brass about production figures. The quotas set by the CCP went higher, and farmers struggled.
Eventually it even caused a massive famine in the country leading to the deaths of millions of Chinese people.
Mao’s vision or the “ Great Leap Forward ” as it was known collapsed.
Then, in 1976, Mao died.
In comes Deng Xiaoping
You can imagine that Deng Xiaoping inherited quite the chaotic and problematic economy. But he also couldn’t just defy the CCP’s top down approach and initiate fixes the way he wanted to. He had to take baby steps.
One of those baby steps was a visit to Japan. To check out a steel plant owned by Nippon Steel Corp.
Yup, the steel dream wasn’t dying with Mao. And this plant was seen as the model that China wanted to build in Shanghai called Baosteel.
But to replicate Japan, China needed $6 billion. This was apparently 36 times more than China’s foreign-exchange reserves back then. But Deng Xiaoping’s idea was: “If we want to do this, let’s do it big.”
A deal was struck. A joint-venture was signed. And China welcomed Japan’s technological support. The economy had begun to open up.
It looks like the US knew what was coming too. Because a classified report by the CIA (Central Intelligence Agency) in 1979 remarked ,
“China should eventually be able to develop a steel industry comparable in size to the steel industries of the U.S., the Soviet Union and Japan.”
The other gamechanger for China was Deng’s visit to Singapore.
Why?
Because a once backwater little fishing island had begun to cement its place in world conversations. When Singapore gained independence in 1965, the share of manufacturing to GDP was 14%. 10 years later, it had jumped to 22% . And Lee Kuan Yew, the first prime minister of Singapore, was at the centre of this transformation.
But beyond that, there was a Chinese influence on Singapore:
In his welcoming remarks [during Deng Xiaoping’s visit], Lee [Kuan Yew] stressed that Singapore’s ethnic Chinese citizens were the sons and daughters of uneducated, landless peasants from Southern China, leading Lee to suggest, as former foreign minister George Yeo has recently phrased it , if Singapore with its “poorly-educated coolies could make good, how much better mainland China could be if the right policies were adopted.”
Deng Xiaoping wanted to learn from the Singapore model of growth and that one visit alone tells you how the thinking had begun to change by 1978. I’m not making that up. Here’s a line from a Singaporean government website :
“The visit also sowed the seeds for the replication of the Singapore model of industrial development in China.”
And one such development was the Special Economic Zone.
Everyone has heard of SEZs. India has them too.
But that’s what China doubled down on. These special enclaves didn’t have the same rules as the rest of China. Different rules applied — freer movement of capital, flexible labour laws, easy land acquisition, consistent, uninterrupted electricity. And quick customs clearances.
You probably know one of the most famous SEZs in China…
Shenzhen!
It was a region that was quite strategically picked out due to its proximity to Hong Kong.
See, Hong Kong was still governed by the British back then. And was a thriving capitalist state with a GDP per capita that was nearly 100x that of Shenzhen. People were wealthy . Businesses were efficient and there was no bureaucracy.
So when Shenzhen became an SEZ, it gave an opportunity for many businesses from across the border to jump in. And by now you’d have realised this but the foreign companies that flooded into these zones in the 1980s were not coming for the Chinese consumer market.
Chinese consumers were still desperately poor. What companies were coming for was cheap, available, productive labour. And a government that had made it its explicit mission to make their lives easy.
As Manoj pointed out during our chat, this is where India keeps missing the plot even today. We talk about attracting foreign investment as though the pitch is our market size and our growth story. And yes, that matters. But what China figured out in the 1980s — before it had any of those things — was that companies first need to be able to operate . Land has to be acquirable. Electricity has to be reliable. A problem has to be solvable without years of bureaucratic navigation. In India, even a politically connected business struggles to acquire land. And tax policy changes and unpredictability makes a long-term manufacturing investment feel like a leap of faith.
But of course things didn’t end here. China was dismantling its carefully orchestrated top-down socialist system to a more decentralized one.
Remember what I told you about agriculture under Mao?
It was collectivist farming. Whatever people produced were just pooled together with no incentive to do more.
But in 1978, something happened.
A group of farmers in a tiny village called Xiaogang signed a secret contract under an oil lamp. They were going to defy the collectivist farming instructions and take a big risk.
Each family would farm their own plot. Some of the harvest would be given up to the government. Some would be pooled into the collective. And anything more would be theirs to keep.
It was blasphemous. They could be executed by the state for this disobedience.
But soon, word of this agreement got out. And guess how?
They had such a bountiful harvest that local CCP officials knew that something was up. The farmers were threatened.
But when Deng Xiaoping heard about this, he decided to make the village a model to be followed.
Procurement quotas were removed. And he essentially told farmers that the CCP would not tell them how much to grow anymore. They could grow as much as they could, sell it in the market, and keep the money.
People had an incentive to produce more. Agricultural output surged. And for the first time in decades, ordinary Chinese people started making more money.
Sidebar: That secret contract is now housed in a museum.
China was changing.
And as Manoj told us, a decentralisation of sorts emerged.
See, most people picture China as a top-down command economy where the central government decided everything and the country marched in lockstep. And that’s what happened till the late 1970s.
But Deng Xiaoping began to shift things a bit. He set broad national goals such as “we want an automobile sector of X scale by this year, we want a semiconductor industry” and then essentially told provinces — “You figure out how to get there”.
And Chinese provinces competed. Ferociously.
Because here’s the thing about the Chinese political system that you should know — bureaucrats are also politicians. Which means, someone handling a province knows that their entire career trajectory to the top of the CCP ranks depends on delivering growth numbers.
So they needed to get investments and build the factories. They needed to show Beijing results and get promoted.
Deng even had a Cat Theory or Philosophy: “I don’t care if the cat is black or white, if it catches the mouse, it’s a good cat.” Basically, to do what it takes to produce the results.
On the other hand, as Manoj highlighted, while India has some remarkable state-level success stories — Tamil Nadu’s electronics manufacturing ecosystem — by and large, the union-state relationship on manufacturing remains inconsistent and deeply underutilised. The incentive for a state government to go out hunting for manufacturing investment is nowhere near as powerful as it was for a Chinese provincial governor whose career depended on it.
And a deeper thinking that Deng Xiaoping brought about by doing this was that a socialist economy need not always be a planned economy and it can be a market one too.
Here’s an excerpt from an interview in 1985 when he was asked about this seeming contradiction:
There is no fundamental contradiction between socialism and a market economy. The problem is how to develop the productive forces more effectively.
…
If we combine a planned economy with a market economy, we shall be in a better position to liberate the productive forces and speed up economic growth.
…
The experience we have gained over the years shows that with the former economic structure we cannot develop the productive forces. That is why we have been drawing on some useful capitalist methods. It is clear now that the right approach is to open to the outside world, combine a planned economy with a market economy and introduce structural reforms. Does this run counter to the principles of socialism? No, because in the course of reform we shall make sure of two things: one is that the public sector of the economy is always predominant; the other is that in developing the economy we seek common prosperity, always trying to avoid polarization. The policies of using foreign funds and allowing the private sector to expand will not weaken the predominant position of the public sector, which is a basic feature of the economy as a whole.
Now you could argue that it was a marriage of convenience and all that, but aren’t all economic-political systems built in that manner? If you’re offering bailouts to corporations (talking about the US here, of course), doesn’t that defy the very principles of free markets and capitalism?
Either way, this “planned economy meets free markets” idea set the tone for China’s boom.
The capital machine
But there’s something else that Manoj pointed out too.
China didn’t really transfer most of the wealth it was creating to the consumers. Rather, the revenue from China’s manufacturing boom went back into the state — particularly into local governments — which then reinvested it into the conditions for more growth. Healthcare. Education. Ports. Railways . Inland-to-port connectivity.
Now hold on…you might be wondering how did the people start getting richer then if the state still controlled the wealth?
Well, the Chinese people didn’t get richer because their existing jobs suddenly started paying western wages; they got richer because hundreds of millions of people were lifted out of near-zero-income farm work and dropped into productive industrial ecosystems.
In 1980, over 80% of China’s population lived in rural areas, scraping by on subsistence farming. By building infrastructure and manufacturing clusters (the SEZs), the state created an insatiable demand for factory workers. Millions of young villagers migrated to cities like Shenzhen where populations zoomed.
Also, in the 1990s, the Chinese state, which owned all the land, started selling “land use rights.” Not the land itself, which remained state-owned, but the right to use it. This created an immediate flood of revenue as factories, real estate developers and foreign investors all wanted access. That money went straight back into industrial subsidies and infrastructure.
It was a supply-side stimulation of the economy on a massive scale. Not demand-led growth where consumers spend and the economy follows. Supply-led growth where the state invested in building the capacity to produce, and the world’s appetite for cheap goods did the rest.
Along came the WTO
In 2001, China joined the World Trade Organisation. And I want you to just think about what this meant.
It meant that China could now sell to every major consumer market in the world on roughly equal terms. For a country that had spent two decades building manufacturing capacity, this was a godsend.
China had a near-inexhaustible supply of cheap, productive labour and it could produce anything and everything for cheaper than the rest of the world — textiles, consumer goods and electronics, anything. Capital flooded into priority sectors like steel too.
Just look at this chart from the Wall Street Journal t hat shows the global steel production. China’s rise after inclusion in the WTO is exponential.
Source: Wall Street Journal
And amidst all this. China was climbing up the value chain.
In the early 1990s, labour-intensive goods such as textiles, clothing, shoes, and hats accounted for almost 40% of China’s total exports. In 2020, that fell to just 14%. Exports of mechanical and electrical products accounted for 44% by then.
And you’ll see how this happened if you simply track the story of any large Chinese conglomerate. Say Huawei .
Even though the company started as a reseller of imported telephone switches in the late 1980s, the Chinese government had identified telecommunications as strategically critical. And with that came state aid (which Huawei says it has never received), policies favouring domestic manufacturers over foreign ones, easier access to contracts in a massive market like China and all of that jazz.
To its credit, Huawei doubled down on its R&D. And being able to offer its telecom equipment at a cheaper rate than foreign rivals didn’t hurt. So much so that in the mid 2010s, the Chinese upstart had become the dominant player in the world.
In short, the state identified a strategic technology. It gave a domestic champion a protected home market to develop in. It flooded that champion with cheap capital. It then helped it go out and conquer the world.
And this model played out in multiple sectors — solar panels, electric vehicles, high-speed rail equipment. The value chain expanded.
But there’s another aspect of this development that Manoj highlighted in the session.
China employed a spray-and-pray model of sorts and tolerated waste.
I’ll explain.
When you hear spray and pray, you’d think they just threw money at everything and hoped something worked, But more than that, it was about identifying where the world was going, which technologies would matter in ten or twenty years, and then flooding those sectors with enough capital that Chinese companies would inevitably end up dominating them, even if the waste along the way was colossal.
China got solar panels wrong the first few times. It produced far more steel than the world needed. It built ghost cities. It wasted billions of dollars on non-productive investment. But in that churn, it also built BYD, Huawei, CATL — companies that now define global industries.
Do you think India can afford such waste?
A wasted rupee of public money is a scandal. A failed government-backed company is an embarrassment. And so we don’t back ten things hoping one works. We try to pick the winner before the race starts. We give subsidies to the chosen few and hope they deliver.
But anyway…
Keeping the value chain
As China’s own costs — including labour and land —- rose through the 2000s and 2010s, something interesting started happening. Manufacturing started moving. To Vietnam. To Malaysia. To Indonesia. And China became one of the largest investors in the region.
Chinese FDI in south east Asia ballooned from just $4 billion in 2010 to US$17 billion in 2023. Cumulatively, over $140 billion was invested between 2010 and 2023.
China was exporting the assembly — the low-skill, low-margin, last-mile work of putting things together. But the intermediate goods, the components, the materials that those assembly plants needed? Those still came from China. Chinese companies invested in assembly plants in Southeast Asia, and those plants were ordering their inputs from Chinese suppliers.
On the face of it, China was losing its manufacturing edge. But China was simply outsourcing the low-value work, extending its value chain and keeping the profitable, complex, high-skill parts of production at home.
We can see this playing out in India too today. Especially in the mobile phone market. And it’s something former RBI governor Raghuram Rajan pointed out a couple of years ago.
In FY18, India exported just $300 million worth of mobile phones. In FY23, we shipped $11 billion worth of them. But, if you include the components needed, our net imports  actually soared by a massive 70% between that period. Components that were coming from China.
Now this is not to debate whether India is doing the right thing by taking up just the assembly end of things. But to point out how China has embedded itself in the supply chain for manufacturing and to what degree. That has been their success.
Because by doing this, China’s trade surplus kept growing. Its exports kept rising. In 2025, it hit a record $1.2 trillion in trade surplus.
Nothing about this was free
There is a version of the China story that gets told everywhere; that China had a strong central government, made bold decisions, built infrastructure, attracted capital, and grew. If only India could be a little more like that.
But that narrative is incomplete.
Because China’s manufacturing miracle came with costs — human, economic, and even structural.
We talked about the spray and pray approach to investing. But the money wasted on unproductive investments was staggering.
One report by Chinese government researchers put the number at $6.8 trillion between 2009 and 2013. We’re talking “ghost cities”, abandoned highways, factories with no activity. Nearly 40% of all investments were “wasted”.
Now that number might be way too high . But no one is denying the waste.
China saw random activity simply because money was available, activity showed up as GDP, and a local official needed to show Beijing a growth number.
In a democracy like India, such wasteful expenditure is going to be questioned, debated, and be a thorn in the side of a ruling party that decided to pursue such a strategy.
Then there are the human costs. Sweatshops operating in the name of factories. Child labour being rampant. Rising wealth inequality where the wealth generated went into state coffers and into the pockets of a relatively small political and business elite; it did not flow broadly to ordinary Chinese households as wages, social security and purchasing power.
And let’s not forget the massive bubble in the property market that the Chinese state allowed to build up and which has now destroyed the wealth of millions of Chinese citizens too.
The problems are plenty.
Where does India fit in today?
Well, we asked Manoj that question — whether the China+1 story is waiting to be scripted in India, and what we can do about it — he was pretty clear in his answer.
We’ve made mistakes and probably keep making them.
For too long, we had reservations for small scale industries. We protected them from competition instead of letting it scale. At one point, over a thousand products were legally reserved for small-scale producers only — meaning large factories couldn’t make them. The message to Indian industry was, “Don’t get too big. Don’t achieve scale”.
Then there was the ease of doing business. We kept electricity cheap for agriculture and expensive for industry . We made land acquisition a decade-long legal battle. We built a tax system that changed its rules frequently. And none of that helped.
But also, we never changed our thinking culture. We never really built the culture of R&D investment . India spends roughly 0.5-0.7% of GDP on research and development — the same number as in the 1990s. And of that, the overwhelming majority comes from the government, not from private businesses. Chinese companies like Huawei spend more on R&D than many Indian industries combined.
Of course India became the services economy for the world — IT, software, back-office work. And this absorbed a highly educated upper layer of our workforce and got the economy to where we are today. But for the millions of young, less-educated Indians entering the workforce every year, there were no factories waiting for them.
Not too late to make the change
Manoj thinks that the South East of Asia still wins over India when it comes to fitting into the China+1 manufacturing play purely based on economics. But we have a real geopolitical moment to make the change. The world genuinely wants to reduce its dependence on China. Political trust has become a manufacturing input in a way it never was before, and India has more of it with the western world than China currently does. The India-EU trade is a sure shot sign of that.
But to really capitalize on this, India needs to fix the ease of doing business in a big way.
Because the thing we also have to remove is that our vaunted demographic dividend — a young, productive workforce — will not last long. We have a window until roughly 2040 before this demographic dividend turns into a demographic burden. That’s fifteen years to build the manufacturing machinery that 5xed China’s per capita GDP over ours.
In Manoj’s words, “ Always rising, never risen” has been our story for long enough. It’s time for India to rise.

Do you remember this viral social media video from 2023? Danielle Lettering’s car had burnt to bits but inside, her Stanley Cup remained untouched. Even the ice cubes in it did not melt.
Source: TikTok via CNA
This is the story of a great product, great marketing, and a great business — Stanley 1913 or Stanley Cups as they’re commonly called. These fancy tumblers with beautiful designs have become a collectible. People want to buy one, and then they want to buy many more Stanley cups in different colors.
But as a brand, Stanley was not always like this. It has shifted identities.
Very few brands have managed to be cool to the younger generation despite being around for 100 years. And Stanley has been one of them.
Now, to understand what the brand did to remain relevant and coveted, let’s go back to where it all began.
The year was 1892. Scottish scientist Sir James Dewar was working on cryogenics. He wanted to maintain chemicals in a flask at a stable temperature. So he placed one glass bottle inside another, and vacuumed out the air between the two to create a flask that could keep the temperature of the chemical inside it stable.
That is how Sir James Dewar invented the world’s first ever vacuum-sealed flask. A vacuum-sealed flask is any flask that keeps cold liquids cold and warm liquids warm for hours. He hired a professional glassblower to commercially produce those flasks and sell them to labs for chemical experiments.
However, Dewar did not patent his invention. Some say it was because he wanted the scientific community to be able to use it freely. Some others say he was disillusioned after his patent battle with Alfred Nobel, the gentleman after whom the Nobel Prize is named.
Either way, the professional glassblower company that was making the Dewar flask for labs improved upon it by adding a metal casing to it. And patented the technology. And named it Thermos. And marketed it well.
So well that Thermos went on to become a category-defining brand. Any flask that can maintain the temperature of the liquid inside came to be known as a Thermos. It was a brand that came to be known as a category definer.
Anyway, back to the central plot of this episode. The Stanley Cups.
American physicist William Stanley Jr. had 129 patents to his name. The most notable was his patent of the world’s all-steel vacuum-sealed bottle. Of course, it was a flask only. But it was different. In fact, we have already discussed three different types of vacuum flasks .
One. the all glass flask that Dewar invented.
Two, the glass flask with metal casing that Thermos patented.
Three, the all-steel flask that Stanley patented.
As an all-metal flask, the Stanley cup had rugged uses. Since it had no glass in its body, there was no fear of breaking if it fell.
So, it was also marketed for its rugged uses by workmen or those engaged in outdoor activities like camping or hiking. For nearly a hundred years, the brand did not change its messaging or its target market.
Even when celebrating its 100th Anniversary in 2012, in a press release, Stanley mentioned how its flasks were used by a policeman who had been a veteran for 30 years or a retired Army soldier.
They introduced a limited edition design to celebrate the century. This new design and all the old ones didn’t look quite different. They were all bulky and dull but robust and useful.
You know, when a brand has been around for a century, and the older generation has been using it for nearly all their lives, the newer generations may not want to use that product. They may not find it cool. They may not vibe with it.
And there was one more piece missing. Stanley was primarily focused on male buyers. But women have outdoor jobs too. They also travel a lot.
And Stanley did not seem like it was making any effort to appeal to either the younger buyers or the women.
But it did innovate its products. In 2016, it introduced a new design of Stanley tumblers, called the Stanley Quenchers. The Quenchers are the popular designs you see today. The Quenchers came with a handle and a straw lid. They looked much classier, even cool.
Stanley had slowly started shifting the narrative.
In one of their listings of the first Quenchers on Amazon, they said — Adventure doesn’t have to be paddling the rapids down a whitewater junction Sometimes, adventure is waking up early to brave the rush hour traffic Luckily, this jumbo insulated cup is ready for adventure wherever you find it.
But these Quenchers were still not their focus. They continued to market Stanley flasks as useful for outdoor workers and adventure activities.
Then came a stroke of luck. Three women, Linley Hutchinson, Ashlee LeSueur, and Taylor Cannon praised the Stanley Quenchers on the Instagram account they ran. Why was it a big deal? The three women were the co-founders of The Buy Guide, an online shopping guide that helps users select the best purchases by making informed recommendations.
The Buy Guide provides a purchase link with its recommendations. Every time a user buys using those links, The Buy Guide makes commissions. It is what you call affiliate marketing.
The management at Stanley was glad that The Buy Guide liked their Quenchers and were recommending it to their followers but it was not willing to participate in The Buy Guide’s affiliate marketing program. They said they did not want to sell through influencers or affiliate marketing channels.
Instead, they insisted that the three founders of The Buy Guide place a wholesale order with a minimum of 10,000 Quenchers. They had never done outright wholesale purchases before. They were a marketing platform, not traders. But they took the risk.
They quickly set up a website, rented a warehouse, and figured out shipping to customers. They sold out the first 5,000 Quenchers in four days. And then they sold the next 5,000 in an hour.
Stanley’s management was beyond thrilled. They requested a meeting with the founders of the Buy Guide and flew them in. In the meeting, the founders told the management that they were selling to the wrong people. That they could market it to women. That the cups were a daily-use item and not just for outdoor use. And that it needed to look good in people’s homes and kitchens.
One founder, Ashlee, went on to say that any brand that isn’t marketing to the 25 to 50 year old woman was really missing the mark. She said that even if you are a men’s clothing line, if you are not finding a way to speak to this 25 to 50 year woman, you are missing the mark. Because those women are the buyers of the economy. They buy for their families, their husbands, and for their businesses.
The partnership with The Buy Guide gave a fresh impetus to Stanley Cups. Demand multiplied as the word-of-mouth publicity grew stronger.
As the management saw how women were demanding the Stanley Cups, they quickly shifted focus. They revamped product design, their website, and their social media to appeal to women.
They transformed the Quencher tumbler into a fashion-forward item, featuring a rainbow of colors and limited-edition patterns. Rather than keeping every color always in stock, they began releasing new colors or collaborations in limited batches – fueling FOMO and urgency. They collaborated with Lionel Messi too.
Stanley’s management was now open to affiliate marketing. In fact, affiliate marketing opened Stanley up to new audiences and allowed customers to connect more directly with the brand.
In 2020, the Quencher overtook the Stanley classic bottle as the brand’s top-selling product.
The brand became so strong that by 2022, people were making videos of their Stanley cups and boasting about it on TikTok and other social media. These were not paid promotions. The Stanley cups became a collectible item. Many people love collecting Stanley cups in all colors. They are eagerly waiting for limited edition designs also. So those people just wanted to show to the world how cool it was to own a Stanley cup. That’s why they were making those videos.
One such TikTok video blew up the marketing game for Stanley in 2023 — the video of burnt car with a Stanley cup intact inside of it. The video raked in over a 100 million views, essentially becoming an ad showcasing the durability of Stanley cups. And the brand itself turned it into a marketing opportunity. They offered to replace the woman’s burnt car and sent her a bunch of new Stanley cups.
The results were visible in the business performance, too. In 2019, Stanley’s annual revenues were around 70-75 million. That number had exploded 10X in four years. Its revenues were $750 million in 2023.
You know, all of this happened because Stanley’s management was receptive to feedback from The Buy Guide. But all of this would not have happened if The Buy Guide had not pushed for Stanley 1913 to reinvent itself. They got lucky, or they would have still been selling tumblers as useful for camping and adventure.
A challenge that Stanley faces and that will only grow stronger is that many brands will now try to replicate what Stanley offers. It is like Tupperware. People love it, but they wouldn’t mind buying a cheaper alternative that looks just as good.
And it is almost funny how Stanley is a brand name owned by so many firms globally. There is an American tool manufacturer company called Stanley Black & Decker. This tool manufacturer recently sued Stanley 1913 for breaching the limits of the use of word Stanley, because it felt the tumbler maker brand had grown beyond its original scope as a drinkware business.
Well, in the tool maker’s defence, Stanley cups have become a cultural phenomenon. It has managed to create a community and a tribe of loyal fans who want to collect Stanley Cups in every edition possible.
From being unable to read the market in changing times to pivoting focus due to valid feedback, Stanley 1913 is a masterclass in product development and marketing strategies.
