For many individual investors, startup investing is like trying to pick a fruit hanging from the highest branch. It looks incredibly tempting, but reaching it is not easy.
If you want to take a bet and if the founders are willing to have you on board, you can invest directly in a startup. But direct startup investing is very different from investing through a regulated investment product.
Take mutual funds, for example. A mutual fund manager pools money from many investors and invests in listed stocks or bonds in accordance with the fund's mandate. It is a regulated product, which means there is a regulator overseeing how the money is pooled, how the product is structured and sold, and what investor protections are in place.
Now, if you are looking for something similar to a mutual fund, but for startups, the options are few and not easily accessible.
It’s no mystery why. Startups are risky. The minimum investment amounts are usually large. The investment is also illiquid, meaning your money could remain stuck for years. You may have to wait a long time for an exit, and in many cases, that exit may never happen.
But curiosity does not go away. Individual investors still want to know whether they can take a bet on startups. What routes are available? What kind of returns can they realistically expect? What are the risks? And what should they watch out for?
The Q&A in this Second Order edition tries to answer all of that. For this, we reached out to our in-house expert, Dinesh Pai, who heads Zerodha Rainmatter Investments, to answer some of the most frequently asked questions. Also, special thanks to RegFin Legal Partners for their inputs on law-related questions.
Q1. How is startup investing different from investing in stocks or mutual funds?
When you invest in a startup, you are putting money into a private company at a very early stage, sometimes before it even has revenue. You are doing this based on your own judgment. In the investing world, this makes you an “angel investor.” (This is different from investing through an Angel Fund, which is a SEBI-regulated investment product: more on that in Q3.)
As an angel investor, you face a few fundamental challenges.
First, information is scarce. Private companies are not required to share their financials with you the way listed companies are. Unless you have a personal relationship with the founders, getting reliable updates on how the business is actually doing can be difficult. Even if you do have that access early on, it can get increasingly difficult as new investors come in and the company’s attention shifts to larger stakeholders.
Second, startup investments are deeply illiquid. There is no marketplace where you can sell your shares tomorrow. There are only a few ways to eventually get your money out: the company goes public through an IPO (Indian startups typically take 8+ years to reach a public listing, and most never get there); a larger company acquires the startup, which might happen in 5–10 years if things go well; or you find another investor willing to buy your shares privately, which is difficult for small stakes in early-stage companies.
Third, there is the problem of dilution. Every time the startup raises more money in future funding rounds, it issues new shares. Your percentage ownership shrinks. Worse, the investors who come in later, typically venture capital (VC) funds, often negotiate special rights for themselves, like the right to get their money back first if things go wrong (called “liquidation preferences”). This can push early angel investors further down the queue when money is eventually distributed.
Q2. If my bet turns out right, what kind of returns can I expect?
The honest answer is: go in assuming you may get nothing back. Anything above that is a bonus.
Many startups fail, and investors can lose their entire investment. That is why the best way to think about angel investing is through a ‘portfolio approach’.
Suppose you invest in 10 startups. You should be prepared for most of them to fail completely. Maybe 7, 8, or even 9 out of 10 may return nothing. The hope is that one successful company gives such a large return that it covers the losses from all the failed ones.
Here is a simple example. Say you invest ₹5 lakh each in 10 startups. That means you invest a total of ₹50 lakh. If 9 startups fail and only 1 works out, that one startup has to return at least ₹50 lakh just for you to recover your original investment. In other words, it has to give you a 10x return on that one investment. For you to make a meaningful profit, that winner may need to return 20x or more.
These outcomes do happen, but they are rare.
And this is not limited to individual investors. It applies to professional investors, too. A US study found that the survival rate of private companies was roughly 35% after 10 years. CB Insights , which tracked over 1,000 seed-stage companies, found that 67% of them fail.
In India, the odds can be even more difficult. Broader industry estimates place the overall startup failure rate at around 90–95% within the first few years of launch.
VCs and institutional investors accept this failure rate because, as we said earlier, startup investing works on a few big winners. As an individual investor, building that kind of portfolio and finding those few winners is much harder. So you should enter startup investing with the clear possibility that the money may never come back.
Q3. What routes are available for individual investors to access startup deals?
There are broadly three ways someone can invest in startups in India.
1. Direct angel investing (not under SEBI’s purview, but legally possible)
There is no regulatory barrier to investing directly in a startup as an individual. If you meet a founder, evaluate the business, negotiate terms, and both parties agree, you can purchase shares in the company. This is a straightforward private transaction between you and the startup.
As for how to actually meet founders, there is no single reliable channel. It can be serendipitous. But intentional effort helps: spend time in places with a high density of startup talent. Incubators, research centres, accelerator demo days, and startup community events are good starting points. Building your network in these circles over time might eventually give you access to real opportunities.
The trade-off is that due diligence, negotiation, legal paperwork, and monitoring are all on you.
2. Through an Angel Fund (SEBI-regulated product)
Angel Funds are regulated by SEBI. They are categorised as Category I Alternative Investment Funds. What do they do? They privately pool money from multiple investors and invest in early-stage startups. The fund manager picks the deals, and investors give consent for the ones they want to bet on. One advantage of this structure is diversification. When you bet on multiple deals proposed by the fund manager, your capital is spread across them.
However, in September 2025, SEBI restricted Angel Funds to accredited investors only. That means, an individual investor would need a net worth of at least ₹7.5 crore (out of which at least ₹3.75 crore must be in the form of financial assets), or annual income of at least ₹2 crore, or a combination (atleast ₹5 crore net worth + ₹1 crore income out of which at least ₹2.5 crore must be in the form of financial assets). So, this route is clearly not available for small investors.
Even before this change, Angel Funds were not a retail product. Regular AIFs require a minimum investor commitment of ₹1 crore. While Angel Funds had a lower requirement of ₹25 lakh, the September 2025 changes removed that and made it eligible only for accredited investors.
To reiterate, the regulator treats start-ups as high-risk investments, illiquid, and unsuitable for investors who may not be able to absorb losses or wait a decade for returns.
3. Informal platforms and groups (unregulated, high risk)
If you come across a few WhatsApp or Telegram groups or online platforms that claim to offer startup deals to individual investors, know that these are not regulated by SEBI. There is no oversight, no disclosure requirement, and no recourse if things go wrong. You are entirely on your own.
Any setup that “pools” capital from multiple investors for the purpose of making startup investments must be registered as an AIF with SEBI. Even when you see words such as SPVs (special purpose vehicles) or LLP (Limited Liability Partnership) or any syndicate models, if they are ‘‘pooling money for investments’’, consider it a red flag. They are not a recognised route as per SEBI’s rules.
See, the startups themselves can be structured as private companies, LLPs, or partnership firms; that is perfectly fine. The issue is when someone pools money from multiple investors to invest in startups without proper SEBI registration.
By the way, there is a distinction between start-up investing and investing in unlisted shares. When you angel-invest in a startup, you are investing at an early stage, often alongside or directly with the founders. When you buy unlisted shares through informal markets, you are usually buying from an existing shareholder at a secondary price, with no relationship to the company or its founders. (See: The risks of investing in unlisted shares. )
Q4. What clauses in the investment agreement determine my rights as an investor?
Several provisions in a typical investment agreement (often called a shareholders’ agreement or SHA) define your rights. These include information and inspection rights (access to financials and a right to undertake audits), board observer or board seat rights, affirmative vote rights where certain important decisions cannot be taken without your approval, anti-dilution protections, pro-rata rights (the right to invest in future rounds to maintain your ownership percentage), and tag-along rights (the right to sell your shares alongside a larger investor).
Here is the catch: most of these protections get renegotiated or restated when a larger institutional investor comes in during a later funding round. The liquidation preferences, anti-dilution protections, information rights, consent rights, and other clauses can all be diluted or removed when VCs with more leverage come to the table.
See, these changes also depend on the terms of your shareholder agreement and the legal structure you have chosen. Whether it is a company governed by the Companies Act, 2013, a partnership firm governed by the Indian Partnership Act, 1932, or a limited liability partnership governed by the Limited Liability Partnership Act, 2008.
But if you invest through an Angel Fund as an accredited investor, the fund manager represents all the individual investors. You sign away individual decision-making rights to the fund manager, who negotiates and votes on your behalf.
Q5. If I invest in a start-up, will I get regular updates about the business?
If you invest in an Angel Fund as an accredited investor, the manager cannot lawfully invest your committed capital in a company without first informing you about that opportunity and getting your consent. After the investment is made, they must keep you updated periodically, typically through half-yearly NAV and portfolio reports, as well as deal-specific updates. If a fund is investing without notifying you, that is a regulatory breach you can flag to the manager and ultimately to SEBI via the SCORES portal.
If you invest directly as an individual angel, there is no such regulatory requirement. Whether you get updates depends entirely on your relationship with the founders and the terms of your investment agreement. Negotiating information rights upfront is one way to address this.
Q6. How much do startups typically raise, and what is the minimum I need to invest?
At a very early stage, there is a pre-seed round. This is when the startup is still at the idea, prototype, or early testing stage, so the amount raised can be relatively small. After that comes the seed round, where the company may have early proof of concept, a basic product, or initial customers. These early-stage seed rounds, which were once in the ₹1–2 crore range, have now grown to around ₹5–7 crore in many cases.
The next major stage is usually Series A. By this point, the company is expected to have stronger traction and is raising money to scale more seriously. Series A rounds can be ₹20–50 crore or more. The cheque sizes usually increase as the company grows.
Now, the minimum investment amount per investor depends entirely on the founder. Founders have to decide how many investors they want on their cap table (the list of all shareholders). Some prefer a clean cap table with just 2–3 early investors writing larger cheques. Others, particularly those who value strategic connections, may allow smaller investments from people who bring specific expertise, industry access, or distribution advantages. In such cases, investments as small as a few lakh rupees are possible.
There is no standard minimum. It is always a negotiation between the investor and the founder.
Q7. Okay, I understand the risks. But if I still want to take a bet on a startup, how do I evaluate a startup?
There is no fixed formula to evaluate a startup. There is no long track record, no standard screener, and no rating agency to guide you. A lot depends on your own judgment.
Ideally, invest in a sector where you have some edge; maybe you understand the industry well, know people who can validate the idea, or have access to good founders. That edge matters. But if you do not have it, look at a few basic things.
First, the team. Do the founders understand the industry? Have they built anything before? Can they handle setbacks? At an early stage, you are mainly betting on the people.
Second, the market. Is the problem real? Is it large enough? Is it growing? A good founder in a tiny market will still struggle.
Third, traction. Growing revenue, repeat usage, strong retention, or organic customer acquisition are real signals. App downloads, signups, and social media buzz are not.
Fourth, business economics. Can the company eventually make more from a customer than it spends to acquire one? Some startups look exciting but the unit economics do not work.
Finally, the roadmap. What does the company plan to do over the next 12–24 months, and is it realistic for the money being raised?
Even after checking all this, startup investing remains uncertain. You are betting that customer behaviour will change, markets will shift, and founders will figure things out. Sometimes great products fail because the timing is wrong. Sometimes, average products succeed because the market is ready.
This is also where small investors need to be especially careful. The best startup deals that tick most of the above points are usually not easily available to small investors. Startups with strong traction and experienced founders tend to attract VC funds and large investors early. These are the folks who write large cheques and also help with hiring, strategy, and future fundraising. If a startup is very attractive, it may not need small investors unless they bring something useful, like industry knowledge or distribution support.
This does not mean every deal available to you is bad. Professional investors, too, may miss good opportunities. But if a deal is easily available to everyone, ask why. Did larger investors pass on it? What risk are you taking that others chose not to?
Your judgment, your network, and your willingness to do proper due diligence are your main tools. Startup investing is not about finding an exciting company. It is about understanding what can go wrong and whether the possible reward is worth that risk.
By the way, if you want to know how VCs think about investing in startups, check out this video .
Q8. If I decide to invest, how do I ensure my liability is limited to the amount I invest and nothing more?
If you invest through an Angel Fund (which is structured as a Category I AIF), your exposure is limited to the amount you have committed to the fund. Angel Funds are typically set up as trusts, and as an investor (or “contributor”), your liability does not extend beyond your committed capital. The fund manager invests on your behalf, and you are not personally liable for the debts or obligations of the startups the fund invests in.
If you invest directly by purchasing equity shares or convertible instruments in a private limited company, your liability is similarly capped at the amount you invested. Similar is the case with LLPs. This is a fundamental feature of ‘limited liability’ entities in India: as a shareholder, you cannot lose more than you put in. One structure to be cautious about: partnerships. In a general partnership, partners may be held personally liable for the partnership’s debts.
Also, just make sure you are not signing on as a personal guarantor for any of the company’s debts (there is no reason for an angel investor to ever do so).

Have you ever heard of a business that started by selling a grocery item but ended up becoming a technology titan?
Well, there are at least two — Wipro and Samsung.
And today, we will take lessons from Wipro on how an organisation manages to pivot into a completely unrelated business and become successful at it.
So both Wipro and Samsung had really humble beginnings. Wipro started as a vegetable and refined oil manufacturer. And Samsung started as a trader of dried fish, locally grown groceries, and noodles.
Today, Wipro is an IT giant with clients all over the world. And Samsung, with its mobile phones, semiconductor chips, and electrical appliances, is one of the most advanced technology companies in the world. Both are stunning examples of a major business pivot.
But our discussion today will revolve around how Wipro reinvented itself and some business lessons along the way.
To appreciate Wipro’s transformation, we must start at the very beginning. The company was founded in 1945 by M.H. Hasham Premji in pre-independence India. Its original name was Western India Vegetable Products Limited – yes, WIPRO is actually an acronym harking back to that old name. Some say WIPRO is an acronym for Western India Palm Refined Oils. Either way, both names are a reference to Wipro’s oil business.
In fact, the current logo of Wipro, a collection of shaded dots making four concentric circles, is a derivation of Wipro’s older sunflower logo, which in turn was a subtle nod to its sunflower oil business.
The business got its first shock in 1966, when the founder passed away unexpectedly. His 21-year-old son, Azim Premji, rushed back from his studies at Stanford to take charge.
As he took over, he diversified Wipro beyond just cooking oil, venturing into consumer products and light engineering. By the mid-1970s, Wipro was producing things like laundry soap and engineering products, alongside edible oils. Wipro had become a modestly successful multi-product company. It was still small, but no longer limited to a single commodity.
Wipro’s move from vanaspati into soaps in the early 1980s was a logical adjacency pivot. It sounds complex, but at its core, adjacency pivot is when you launch a new product that shares some traits with your older products. For example, when ITC wanted to diversify beyond cigarettes, entering the consumer products space was easier. ITC was already sourcing tobacco from its network of farmers. So it could lean on to the same network to source other agricultural products to introduce its new line of processed foods.
On the same lines, Wipro launched Santoor in 1985 as a value sandalwood-and-turmeric soap, initially focused on South India. It didn’t become an overnight success, but over time, smarter positioning helped it grow into one of India’s top soap brands. The Santoor Mom ads are discussed even today.
But Wipro also made a pivot that was not adjacent to its existing businesses.
The year was 1977. India introduced new foreign investment rules that put two choices before the multinationals operating in India.
They could either dilute majority ownership and share technology or exit the country.
IBM decided to exit, abruptly creating a huge void in India’s computing market. At that time, IBM virtually was the computer market in India. Its departure meant Indian businesses and government agencies suddenly had nowhere to buy modern computers. Azim Premji saw an opportunity.
He steered Wipro into the nascent information technology sector, a realm far removed from cooking oil. And to signal the pivot, the company’s name was changed to Wipro Products in 1977. After a few years of groundwork, Wipro launched India’s first indigenous personal computer in 1981, around the same time when personal computers were just taking off globally.
And in 1982, Wipro Products became Wipro Ltd.
Wipro’s computers were a success in the local market, which was a big validation for an Indian company innovating in technology. But Wipro did not stop at hardware; It started a software division too.
By the way, if you haven’t already noticed, the Santoor soap launch that we discussed earlier happened while Wipro was launching its software business.
And by the end of the 1980s, Wipro had transformed into a full-fledged IT company, while it still retained its other businesses. The consumer business ensured a stable cash flow while Wipro took risky bets in its tech ventures.
Just when Wipro had become a big name in the tech sector, India liberalized its economy in 1991, welcoming foreign investment and competition once more. This meant IBM and others could enter India and threaten Wipro’s position. So Wipro started looking beyond India. Western companies, looking to lower costs, were happy to outsource certain IT work to India. This was the labour-cost arbitrage that Wipro, along with Infosys, TCS, and others capitalized on to make India the IT hub of the world.
During the 1990s and early 2000s, Wipro evolved into a full-blown IT services and outsourcing provider. This strategic shift was enormously successful. Revenues exploded. As per Wipro’s oldest annual report that I could find, which was financial year 1996, it earned close to Rs 1200 crores in revenues, and roughly half of that came from the tech business. And today, as per its annual report for FY2025, it closed the year with Rs 89,000 crores in revenues. But all that is just IT revenues now.
In 2013, Wipro demerged all its non-IT business into a separate private entity. It is called Wipro Enterprises. This consumer business is sizable, too. Its revenues were nearly Rs 17,000 crores in FY2024. It makes sense to separate the two businesses. After all, while the IT business became bigger and got all the spotlight, the consumer business continued to chart its own growth by launching new products and acquiring other consumer businesses in India and abroad. And the consumer business has been large and as diverse as you could imagine — Wipro sells baby care products as well as furniture!
By the way, around the time of demerging the consumer business, Wipro even sold off its original Sunflower Vanaspati cooking oil brand to Cargill, symbolically closing the chapter on its very first product line.
So, what does Wipro look like today?
It remains a name synonymous with IT services globally, and it also enjoys a strong reputation in the lighting industry. And the Santoor brand continues to invoke nostalgia and the feel-good factor among consumers.
Very few businesses have managed to function like a conglomerate. Wipro has managed to do it successfully, even though its IT business remains in the spotlight. Part of the reason why they managed to be successful is that they could sense when it was the right time to spin off the non-IT business. It ensured that there were two separate management teams, each dedicating full focus to either the IT or the consumer business.
And a major reason is that Wipro identified the shifting external landscape and seized opportunities as they presented themselves, whether it was IBM’s exit in 1977 or India’s liberalization of the economy in 1991.

On Sunday, May 10, 2026, Prime Minister Narendra Modi made an appeal:
Translated: “In the interest of the nation, we will have to decide that for a year, no matter what function or program takes place at home, we will not buy gold jewellery, we will not buy gold. To save foreign currency, our patriotism is challenging us.”
While the Prime Minister’s words targeted physical gold jewelry, the economic logic indirectly extends to paper gold investments as well.
All gold-related investment products in India are ultimately linked to physical gold, except Sovereign Gold Bonds (which are not open for fresh issuance anyway). Fresh buying of gold ETFs and gold mutual funds creates physical demand for gold.
The PM’s statement, at the end of the day, is still just an appeal. But the fact that the entire country was talking about it tells you how deep gold runs in the Indian psyche. And in all those conversations, almost nobody was talking about what gold does inside an investment portfolio.
That got me thinking: what would our portfolios have looked like if there were no gold in them at all?
I took four portfolios - two with gold, two without gold; and ran them for 30 years from 1996 to 2026.
‘A’ vs ‘B’ tells you what 10% gold does to a simple portfolio of equity and debt. ‘C’ vs ‘D’ tells you the same when you already have some international diversification (US equity).
(Methodology* of analysis at the end of the story)
1. Adding gold boosted returns, more often than not
We are looking at a 10% gold allocation in a portfolio. At that level, gold is not going to dramatically boost returns, nor is it going to hurt them.
Gold is a commodity, not a cash-generating asset. Pushing the allocation well beyond 10-20% just to chase higher returns would be the wrong reason to hold gold (unless you want to bet), and a different conversation altogether.
Now, within that allocation, adding gold was a better choice than not adding it in the last 30 years. Here’s the performance of portfolios with a starting capital of Rs 1 lakh.
See, it’s just based on one long 30-year period of entering in April 1996 and exiting in April 2026. We cannot conclude from this one data point alone.
So, we looked at the 10-year periods between 1996 and 2026. Like April 1996 to March 2006, May 1996 to April 2006, June 1996 to May 2006… all the way to May 2016 to April 2026.
In about 160 of 242 such periods, the gold portfolio (B) delivered better returns than the no-gold portfolio (A).
Similar is the case for portfolios C &D as well. So, we can say that portfolios with gold have, more often than not, come out ahead.
2. Adding gold reduced volatility
Volatility tells you how sharp and how frequent the ups and downs in your portfolio are. A portfolio that swings 5% one month, drops 8% the next, and jumps 6% after that has high volatility.
What our analysis showed is that every time gold was part of the portfolio, the volatility was lower. Over the full 30-year stretch, and across all 10-year periods we tested between 1996 and 2026, the gold portfolio was less volatile than the no-gold portfolio. Every single time.
And it wasn’t just volatility. In finance, there’s a metric that’s arguably more useful than returns alone: risk-adjusted return. It measures how much return you earned for every unit of risk you took. And on this measure too, the gold portfolios came out ahead in every single period we tested.
Gold has historically had a low correlation with equity and debt. It means it often moves differently, which can reduce overall portfolio volatility.
3. Gold cushioned the fall during stress times
Finally, let’s come to the role gold is best known for: the yellow metal is often expected to hold up better when equities are under stress.
We checked three major stress periods: the dot-com crash, the 2008 financial crisis, and the COVID sell-off. In each case, portfolios with gold fell less than those without.
The difference wasn’t dramatic, and that’s expected. Gold was only 10% of the portfolio, so it could not magically protect the entire portfolio from falling. Just that gold portfolios fell a little less.
But that still matters. When markets are down, and an investor needs liquidity, gold can sometimes be the asset they sell rather than being forced to exit equity at the worst possible moment. That’s not a small thing.
There is an important caveat, though. Gold is not a perfect hedge. It does not always rise when equities fall, and it should not be treated as guaranteed crash insurance. Erb and Harvey’s well-known 2013 paper, The Golden Dilemma , challenged many popular claims about gold, including that it is always an inflation hedge, currency hedge, or safe haven. It all depends on the periods we have chosen to study gold.
Finally..
Now, coming back to our original question: what if gold weren’t there in your portfolio?
Summing up all our points, a portfolio without gold would have generated slightly lower returns, higher volatility, lower risk-adjusted returns, and offered less cushion during market stress.
Will these patterns hold in the future? Not necessarily. No one can say that with certainty. But going by what actually happened in India over three decades, we at least know what to possibly expect, and what not to expect, from gold as part of our portfolio.
Methodology:
We ran a monthly INR portfolio simulation from April 1996 to April 2026, starting with ₹100,000. NIFTY 500 TRI was used as the Indian equity proxy; debt, by the Post Office 1-Year Time Deposit rate converted to monthly returns; gold, by the RBI monthly average gold prices; and US equity, by the S&P 500 Total Return Index converted to INR using USD/INR. Monthly asset returns were calculated as the current month's level minus the previous month's level, and portfolios were rebalanced annually at December-end (taxes not considered, for simplicity). CAGR was calculated from the starting and ending portfolio values, volatility was calculated as the standard deviation of monthly portfolio returns, annualized by multiplying by √12, risk-adjusted return was measured as CAGR divided by annualized volatility, and max drawdown was the largest fall from a previous portfolio peak.

Aditya Birla Group has at least four European-sounding apparel brand names — Peter England, Allen Solly, Louis Phillipe, and Van Heusen.
Of these, Peter England has an Irish origin. Allen Solly has English origins. And Van Heusen is from the US. Aditya Birla Group acquired the rights to sell these brands in India. But the highlight is Louis Phillipe. Louis Phillipe is an India-born brand. And its story goes like this.
There is a British brand called Coats Group. It held a subsidiary in India. It was a slightly more complicated holding structure, but for simplicity’s sake, let’s call it a subsidiary. That subsidiary was called Madura Garments. In 1989, Madura Garments introduced a new menswear brand called Louis Philippe.
What’s striking here is that it sounds like an actual person’s name. I mean, if you look at brands like Giorgio Armani and Louis Vuitton, they are both labels that have the same name as their founders.
But Louis Philippe is not the founder’s name. It was, in fact, inspired by King Louis Philippe of France, just meant to sound fancy, and make customers feel fancy.
The French-sounding Indian brand worked well for Madura Garments. That is why it also acquired the rights to introduce Allen Solly, Van Heusen, and Peter England in the next few years in India. Of course their origins were foreign. Madura Garments, perhaps, figured that a foreign brand name worked, regardless of where it originated.
It was a different story why Madura Garments could not sustain on its own, and the Coats Group had to sell it to Aditya Birla Group. They suffered losses and financial difficulties due to worker strikes and other issues. And Aditya Birla Group, with its deep pockets, had the wherewithal to pull the business out of its difficulties and capitalize on the following its brands had cultivated. And that is how the four western-sounding brands, Louis Philippe, Van Heusen, Allen Solly, and Peter England landed in Aditya Birla Group’s portfolio.
Now, Louis Philippe was among the first ones, if not the first one, to have a foreign-sounding name despite originating in India. Many other Indian brands followed. Blackberrys, Park Avenue, and Monte Carlo, are all Indian apparel brands with European names.
This practice of deliberately giving foreign names to brands is very common across product categories. There is Bella Vita (which sounds Italian) in perfumes. Da Milano and Kompanero in bags. And La Opala (French, anyone?) in crockery.
There is some fascination with these foreign names. Somehow, we feel more assured reading these names. They are somehow suggestive of quality.
One way to think about this is that, as humans, we don’t always evaluate a product for its material or engineering. In all likelihood, we may not even know how to evaluate the product. Honestly, how confident can you be in identifying the quality of a cloth or even something as simple as a pomegranate?
So we do something faster. We use shortcuts. And one of the fastest shortcuts in modern marketing is the implied origin of a brand. Researchers call this the country-of-origin effect: the idea that place associations can shape perceived quality and status. Several studies have found that consumers rate foreign brand names higher in terms of technology, quality, and esteem, even while expressing pride in Indian manufacturing. Foreignness came with a credibility halo.
In experiments on “foreign branding,” researchers have shown that simply pronouncing or spelling a brand name in a foreign language can trigger cultural stereotypes and alter product perceptions. Mind you, stereotypes can be positive. When a foreign-sounding name creates more trust, it is because of a positive stereotypical association.
And that is why, an Italian-sounding Bella Vita or Da Milano, and French sounding La Opala make sense despite originally being Indian brands.
The country-of-origin effect, in fact, can differ across products. You must have seen an Indian machine coming with a tag that says something like “made with German engineering” or a bag that uses Italian leather. So, basically, the western-ness of a brand varies across product categories.
By that virtue, do Indian names stand out in any category?
Sure when it comes to ethnic wear, we may prefer Indian names like Manyavar, Neeru’s, etc. But when it comes to “dressing for work”, it is also seen as a statement of upward social mobility — first job, first promotion, first big-city identity. Those moments are often seen as modern and corporate. And in India, corporate speaks English, even if the person wearing the shirt doesn’t.
But would you call it our colonial mentality?
Colonial mentality, by the way, is the internalized attitude of ethnic or cultural inferiority felt by people as a result of colonization. Meaning, when you as an Indian assume that a white person could be better at English, has a better dressing sense, or in general is smart, only because he or she is white, you might be exhibiting colonial mentality.
So, does that explain the allure of western or European-sounding names?
Maybe. Partly. Generation after generation, Indians have equated English with education, status, and authority. So it could be that.
But then you also have a post-1991 globalized India that led to an influx of a lot of foreign products. Consumers actually witnessed foreign brands being better at quality than their Indian counterparts. Indian businesses did not have technology to even try to offer better products. Today, after 35 years, Indian brands are often at par in terms of quality, which is why you find many new-age Indian brands proudly flaunting Indian sounding names.
But it’s not always the case. And often, the name-perception debt might be too heavy for a brand to take a chance with a local sounding name. It could be a proud made-in-India brand, and still, its English or French name could have a stronger consumer pull than an Indian name.
Having said that, a deeper analysis of whether a western or European-sounding name helps reach a wider audience may not really be needed.
There is research to suggest that some American brands have a French name on purpose. Tresemme, for example, is an American brand that was given a French name. Then there is a French brand of casual apparel called American Vintage. It has American in its name, but it is not American.
So, no matter which country you reside in, you will always have a perception of certain things being of superior quality based on their indicative origin or based solely on the fact that they are from foreign countries. The French know their perfumes. Watches are the best in Switzerland. Like that. It does not have to do with colonialism.
The underlying is that foreign-sounding names feel more aspirational and are suggestive of quality. Sure, foreign names create a desired perception among consumers. But does that translate into actual business?
Well, honestly, it is hard to attribute any part of the revenues to brand names. But it is safe to say that foreign names often signal premium quality. They borrow an “imagined origin” that makes shoppers feel safer about paying more.

Every time you fill petrol at a pump in India, you’re also filling up with a little bit of sugarcane juice.
Or a fermented type of sugarcane juice.
Since 2022 , every litre of petrol sold in India has had at least 10% ethanol blended into it. At first, you probably never even realised that. The fuel pump attendant didn’t tell you anything. Your vehicle’s engine didn’t complain. And somewhere in a sugarcane field in Uttar Pradesh or Maharashtra, a farmer was quietly part of your morning commute.
But slowly, that 10% became 20% and people started noticing and talking about it. Questions were raised not only on why India was doing this but also the unintended consequences.
And now, since it looks like India wants a 100% ethanol-blend sooner rather than later, it’s time we talk about it too. The why, the how, and the should we?
Why does India want this so badly?
Let’s start with a number that tends to make economists queasy – $120 billion .
That’s what India spends roughly every year on importing crude oil now. Around 85% of the country’s total oil requirement comes from the Gulf plus Russia. Sure, we refine crude oil and export it too. But we consume a lot of it. We’re the third largest consumers in the world.
And this puts us in a tough spot. Because every time crude prices spike due to a conflict in the Gulf, or OPEC (the oil producer’s cartel) decides to squeeze supply, India’s import bill balloons.
Your fuel bills get more expensive. That translates into inflation across goods (because goods get transported from one place to another). And the higher demand for dollars to pay these bills leads to the rupee coming under pressure.
There’s a ripple effect that hurts our economy.
And this energy dependence becomes India’s bottleneck.
But add some ethanol into the equation and things change.
But what’s ethanol?
Think of ethanol as fermented alcohol. You can make it from foodgrains such as rice, wheat, or maize. And sugarcane too.
Anyway, if you blend 20% ethanol into every litre of petrol sold in India, you effectively replace 20% of your crude oil requirement with something you can grow right here. With pretty much no shortage to worry about.
And that’s the simple reason why India wants to do this. It’s to reduce our import bill. The government’s estimates say that between 2014 and 2024, we saved ₹85,000 crores thanks to increased use of ethanol.
Sidebar: Another government statement pegged it at ₹ 1.4 lakh crores .
But what that also translates into is the added advantage of energy security, of course. If we have to rely less and less on imports, we become “atmanirbhar” (self-reliant) in ensuring that our cars and trucks keep moving on the roads.
There’s one more thing beyond this. There’s a farmer angle too. India has about 5 crore ( pdf ) sugarcane farmers. Ethanol gives them another buyer — the oil companies — for their produce. And the support for these farmers is much needed as my colleagues over at the Daily Brief pointed out recently in a story tracing India’s history with sugarcane.
Either way, imagine if we gradually move higher from 20% ethanol blends. To 50%. And then to 100%.
That’s what the government is trying to solve — energy and agriculture. Whether it achieves both is a separate debate.
Can India actually pull off a 100% ethanol fuel economy?
Things get interesting and complicated here.
Firstly, India’s progress on the blending targets have been quite spectacular. In a country where delays are common, India reached 10% ethanol blending in 2022, five months ahead of schedule. And then the government revised the original 20% target from 2030 to 2025 and is said to have achieved that too
So the momentum is real.
But 20% blending is one thing. A full transition to 100% ethanol is a different beast entirely.
The supply question
To be fair, we shouldn’t be worrying about the supply needed for E100 just yet. It’ll be quite a while before we actually get there. India will first have to get to a 30% blend, then maybe a few more pit stops along the way before 85% is reached, and then the 100%.
Right now, the demand from E20 blending is 10-12 billion litres of ethanol annually. But the government says that the country has installed capacity for 20–21 billion litres annually. And that means we can comfortably achieve the 30% blend. We don’t need to worry.
What we do need to keep in mind though as the use of ethanol inches higher and higher is a bunch of other things.
For starters, what happens when crops have a bad year?
See, sugarcane production in India is heavily dependent on the monsoon. A bad year with lower rainfall and delayed sowing hurts ethanol supply. For instance, in 2023 , a weaker-than-expected sugarcane harvest forced the government to temporarily restrict sugar mills from diverting cane to ethanol. We didn’t want to run out of sugar.
And variations of this could happen across other crops in the ethanol value chain — rice, maize, etc.
Which means that since ethanol competes with food, food wins. And that’s a supply risk.
Food security, water, sustainability et al
Here’s what is happening right now.
Farmers are increasingly turning to crops that they know will have a highly interested, often lucrative buyer in the ethanol market.
Maize has been sown across 91.89 lha [lakh hectares] so far in the 2025-26 kharif season, according to data from the Department of Agriculture and Farmers Welfare. This is up from 83.15 lha in the same period last year and a 10.5 per cent year-on-year rise. Compared to the normal sowing (five-year average) for this period, the increase is even steeper at 16.3 per cent.
[…]
Sugarcane, another important ethanol feedstock, has seen an increase of 1.64 lha.
But why is that a problem?
Well, land is finite. So farmers are constantly operating in a framework of tradeoffs. If sugarcane and maize are given preference, it’s at the cost of some other crop. And in India, maize and sugarcane are eating into acreage that traditionally grew pulses such as tur and oilseeds.
That means India will inadvertently shrink its domestic production of essential proteins and fats.
And that puts us at the mercy of global supply chains for food staples and oils too.
And we’ve seen this story play out in other parts of the world. When crops are diverted from food production to fuel production, food prices can rise. In the US, when corn-based ethanol production scaled up dramatically in the 2000s, global corn prices spiked, affecting food security in parts of the developing world ( pdf ).
To be fair, India’s government has tried to draw a clear line and has directed using damaged food grain and surplus sugarcane for ethanol, not diverting food crops. But in practice, that line gets blurry when ethanol prices are attractive.
It eventually turns into a problem.
There are other consequences too. Such as the water problem.
Take sugarcane for instance which accounts for around 30-35% of ethanol in India.
One thing worth knowing though is that sugarcane cultivation guzzles water by the truckloads. Behind every 1 litre of ethanol from sugarcane, there’s roughly 3,000 litres of water ( pdf ) And that mammoth number matters in a country where water stress is already acute.
And scaling up ethanol production means scaling up water consumption. That trade-off doesn’t disappear just because the end product is a “green fuel.”
Speaking of green fuels, is ethanol really green?
The short answer is that compared to petrol, ethanol does produce fewer particulate emissions, less carbon monoxide, and lower overall greenhouse gas emissions per kilometre. That’s when you look at what comes out of the tailpipe alone.
But the full picture is trickier.
I already highlighted the potential water problem. Sugarcane is a water guzzler but it’s not just that. The effluents from sugar mills are often dumped straight into rivers which pollutes them. In fact, government think-tank NITI Aayog’s report from a few years ago said that 70% of water in Uttar Pradesh is polluted and unsustainable sugarcane production is one of the key reasons why.
Then there’s also the bigger worry of land emissions.
If we want to massively expand the production of agricultural produce that goes into making these biofuels, that would end up in forests being cleared to make way for cultivation. That will exacerbate climate change and will be a disaster.
So India’s land-use patterns for agriculture and forest cover will be something that’s worth tracking as biofuels pick up steam.
Then there’s the infrastructure question
Ethanol is not the same as petrol, and your car’s engine is not indifferent to what goes in.
Older petrol engines were not designed to handle high ethanol concentrations. Ethanol is slightly corrosive and can damage rubber seals, fuel lines, and certain metal components if the engine hasn’t been designed for it.
Here’s something a NITI Aayog report ( pdf ) said a couple of years ago:
A project to study the suitability of 20% ethanol-gasoline blend (E20) with in-use vehicles was undertaken by Automotive Research Association of India (ARAI), Indian Institute of Petroleum (IIP) and Indian Oil Corporation (R&D) during 2014-15, with a funding from Department of Heavy Industry (DHI) [8]. Material compatibility tests revealed that the metals and metal coatings had no issue with E20. Elastomers (NBR/PVC blend and Epichlorohydrin) had inferior performance with E20 compared to neat gasoline. Plastic PA66 had a drop in tensile strength after use with E20. In the vehicle level studies, fuel economy decreased up to 6% (depending on the vehicle type) on an average basis.
And such news could even mean pushback from the public. Because as Magnus Bergquist, Senior Lecturer in the Department of Psychology at the University of Gothenburg, told Mongabay
“In a recent series of experimental studies, I found that perceived unfairness is a stronger barrier to supporting environmental policies than perceived ineffectiveness or perceived cost. Moreover, when a policy is perceived as unfairly implemented and unfairly distributed (uneven costs), it erodes trust in policymakers.”
Imagine when this goes to E30 and beyond. Public perception could play a key role.
And beyond this, the government will need car manufacturers to be ready too. With cars that can handle different fuels. And even a supply chain that can handle ethanol’s different storage requirements — tanks and all. That will require significant investment too.
Anyway, at the end of the day, change is coming. E30, E85, and eventually E100. The only question is how we deal with the trade-offs. That will be India’s challenge.
